problem: Profilers and performance models tell a developer where a GPU kernel is slow, but they do not say what code to change. Translating a Roofline plot, a stall report, or a list of hardware counters into an edit is still a manual task that needs architectural expertise. We ask whether an LLM, given the right runtime diagnostics, can write code edits that are correct and faster.
importance: Few developers have routine access to vendor engineers or system architects, so most are left with large volumes of diagnostic data and no clear next step. LLMs alone do not fill this gap: when we gave an LLM only the GPU source code, it produced no optimization that improved performance. Performance context is therefore the missing input, and the diagnostics users already collect can supply it.
challenges: Prior LLM work on code optimization relies on static analysis or prompt tuning, so it never sees stalls, occupancy, or memory throughput, which are the signals that decide real performance. Adding those signals is not a matter of pasting a profile into a prompt. Raw PC-sampling output for one 41-line kernel is 990 MB, far beyond any model's context window. The three diagnostic sources also answer different questions and can point to different causes, and hundreds of hardware counters exist with no rule for which ones matter. Finally, an LLM can write edits that compile but do not target the actual bottleneck, and nothing in the model itself checks that.
approach:
We first built Opal, which combines three complementary sources: Roofline analysis says whether a kernel is compute- or memory-bound, PC stall sampling says which source lines stall and why, and hardware-counter analysis says which events correlate with slowdown across inputs. Opal extracts only the salient signals from each source, which cuts the PC-sampling input for one kernel by 99.9% to under 6 KB, and places them in a structured prompt.

The prompt requires the LLM to link every edit to the diagnostic it addresses and to list the edits it considered unsafe and did not apply. OPTIMAS extends this into a multi-agent pipeline that selects the kernels covering 80% of runtime, profiles, builds the prompt, calls the LLM, compiles, and validates the output bit-for-bit against reference results. It works with commercial models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro) and a locally hosted model (Llama 3.1 70B). We also defined Evidence-Aligned Reasoning (EAR) metrics, which measure whether each edit cites diagnostic evidence and lands on the identified hot spot, not only whether it runs faster.
impact:
Across 1,640 Opal experiments on eight GPU applications and 68 input configurations, every generated version but one passed the benchmark's correctness tests, and edits reduced execution time by up to 87.6% (33.3% on average). OPTIMAS, published at KDD 2026 (18.5% acceptance rate), generated correct code in all 3,410 experiments and improved performance in over 98.82% of them, with average gains of 8.02% to 79.09% on NVIDIA GPUs.

One optimization iteration takes under 10 minutes, while collecting the profiles for SW4Lite took about 16 to 24 hours. The full set of GPT-5 experiments cost $9.83 in API fees, about $0.085 per experiment. We released the prompts, LLM responses, and runtime measurements for all 3,410 experiments as an open dataset on Zenodo.

problem: HPC users must choose node counts, GPU counts, task binding, and power settings, and each choice moves runtime, energy, and variability in different directions. We identify three questions that users ask repeatedly: what configuration to start with, how to change a run that missed its goal, and what will happen if one parameter changes. Existing tools answer at most one of these questions, and none lets a domain expert state rules a configuration must not break.
importance: A configuration that is best in one scenario can show up to 4x variability under slightly different conditions, so performance is a trade-off space, not a single target. Users who guess wrong either request too few nodes and risk termination, or too many and waste energy and allocation. Facility operators face the same trade-off at system scale, where scheduling changes cannot be tested on a production machine without service interruptions.
challenges: Each existing method solves one piece: autotuners search for one objective and return one configuration; generative models synthesize plausible configurations but cannot minimally edit a specific prior run; counterfactual methods such as DiCE edit a run but assume classification and do not check domain constraints; and predictive models estimate outcomes but cannot generate alternatives. Combining them means separate models plus rules to stop them from contradicting each other. Without constraint checking, a model can return a configuration that looks valid but cannot run, such as 16 GPUs on fewer than 4 nodes of Marconi100, which has 4 GPUs per node. Production telemetry adds its own obstacles: it has missing entries, inconsistent counters, and traces of billions of rows, which makes surrogate models unstable and slow to train, while scheduling simulators do not model the machine's power and cooling response at all.
approach:
WANDER unifies prediction, counterfactual generation, and query-driven recommendation behind one query interface, and scores each suggestion using prediction uncertainty, agreement with a causal model, and similarity to historical data. COMPASS formalizes the three user questions as recommend, reconfigure, and what-if queries, which map to inverse modeling, counterfactual generation, and forward prediction. It solves all three with one loss, Conditional Constrained Counterfactual Generation, which encodes validity, closeness to the user's baseline, user-specified constraints, and diversity in a single objective.

COMPASS labels each suggestion as trusted, caution, or unsupported, lists the observed samples that support it, and, when no data supports a region, names configurations to run next. To choose node counts under runtime-power trade-offs, we pair attention-based embeddings of job telemetry with multi-objective Bayesian optimization and active sample acquisition. With collaborators at ORNL, NREL, LLNL, and Colorado State, we extended the ExaDigiT digital twin with scheduling (S-RAPS), so scheduling policies and incentive structures can be evaluated against simulated power and cooling before deployment.
impact:
Integrated with a validated scheduler simulator on production traces, COMPASS cut average job turnaround time by 25.53% and allocated 67.77% fewer nodes than ModelX, a state-of-the-art ML-based scheduler; against the user-specified baseline, the reductions are 65.93% and 80.93%. Fewer nodes per job is the mechanism: it raises system availability and shortens queueing delay. On real hardware, configurations COMPASS labels trusted ran within 13.31% of their predicted execution times, and it scaled to a 1.3-billion-sample, 126 GB trace with up to 80x faster inference than the GReaT generative baseline.

On the Adastra production dataset, attention-based embeddings improved Pareto hypervolume by 37% over direct regression, and active sampling kept results stable with 50 to 75% of the data while cutting end-to-end time by 27%. In the S-RAPS digital twin, which loads public traces from Frontier, Marconi100, Fugaku, Lassen, and Adastra, an ML-guided policy gave the lowest turnaround time and energy-delay product under high load on Fugaku.

problem: We want to predict how an application will run on a new system, or how a new application will run on a known system, without collecting a full training set for each pair. Building a performance model for every new system and application takes days or weeks of data collection. We therefore reuse data and models that already exist and adapt them with only a few samples from the target.
importance: New architectures arrive about every six months, and users, schedulers, and procurement teams must decide which platform to use before anyone has measured it. Configuration choices matter: prior studies report slowdowns of up to 4x when resources are configured poorly. A prediction that needs only a few target runs turns a weeks-long measurement campaign into a short pilot.
challenges: Transfer learning methods such as fine-tuning and linear probing assume that source and target datasets have the same feature names, counts, and order, or that one is a strict subset of the other. HPC data breaks that assumption, because hardware counters differ by architecture: L3-cache counters on Intel systems do not exist on IBM BG/Q. When the features do not match, existing methods cannot adapt the source model and must retrain from scratch, and a few samples are too few to train a model from scratch. Cross-platform models built on raw data or static hardware descriptions such as core counts also miss dynamic properties such as memory bandwidth, so they do not extend to unseen machines.
approach:
We first cast the task as relative performance: the ratio of an application's runtime on a target machine to its runtime on a reference machine. The ratio removes effects such as iteration count, so a model learns how each machine runs the same work. We then studied which models transfer best with few target samples, and found that few-shot learning, multi-source models, and LLM-generated samples each improve cross-platform transfer.

xAMM uses attention to turn raw counter samples into embeddings, and builds an Abstract Machine Model (AMM) for each machine from RAJAPerf benchmark runs: a single vector that summarizes its bandwidth, compute intensity, and scaling. ModelX handles datasets whose features do not match. It first learns an input alignment that maps target features into the source model's space, then, if unaligned features remain, stacks a residual network trained on the few target samples. A severity measure tells us when alignment alone is enough and when the residual model is needed.
impact:
ModelX outperformed fine-tuning, linear probing, and few-shot retraining in all experiments across 11 HPC and 4 ML datasets, and it matched a fully supervised model trained on up to 100x more target data using only 1-5% of the target samples. For OpenMC, 4 new samples were enough to predict performance from Intel Sandy Bridge to IBM BG/Q and back. Used to pick job configurations on real job traces, ModelX cut average turnaround time by 71% and the resources needed for the same turnaround by 42%.

xAMM reduced the prediction error (MAPE) of XGBoost by 49.64% for CPU-to-CPU and 99.07% for CPU-to-GPU prediction across LLNL's Quartz, Ruby, and Corona, compared to training on raw data.

problem: HPC performance data comes as tables: one row per run, one column per configuration or counter. Standard models learn from correlations among columns within a row and ignore how rows relate to each other, even though runs with similar settings tend to have similar runtimes. Source code has the same blind spot: its structure is a tree, but most models read it as flat features. We ask whether representing runs, anomalies, and code as graphs and trees gives better predictions, and, when the data is too scarce to learn from, whether generative models can synthesize more of it.
importance: Schedulers use runtime estimates as a hard cutoff: a job that runs past its estimate is evicted and sent to the back of the queue, and an overestimate leaves nodes idle. Better embeddings improve these predictions without extra feature engineering, which today costs time and needs a human in the loop. Finding the runs slowed by contention or hardware problems lets users and facilities fix the cause sooner. Developers learn about performance only after they run the code; a prediction from source code alone lets them catch a slowdown when they write the change. Every one of these models needs many samples, and each sample means running the application again.
challenges: Graph neural networks work well when a graph already exists, as in social networks, but a performance dataset has no graph; one must be built, and the choice of edges decides what the model can learn. Performance tables also have missing counter values and arrive as streams, so tree-based and deep tabular models such as XGBoost and TabNet either fail on missing values or must be rebuilt for every new sample. For code, absolute runtime depends on the architecture, the input, and the OS, none of which appear in the source, and no large labeled set of programs with measured runtimes existed. For synthetic data, there is no ground truth to check each generated sample against, and existing quality metrics such as KL divergence measure distribution similarity, which does not necessarily predict whether a model trained on the data will generalize.
approach:
PinG makes each run a node and connects it to its N most similar runs by cosine similarity. A self-supervised GNN (GraphSAGE) then refines the edges and learns an embedding per node, which a simple feed-forward network uses for regression; a new, unlabeled run can be placed next to its neighbors without rebuilding the graph. For anomalies, we built graphs from Chimbuko's provenance database: each execution event is a node linked to its three nearest events, anomaly detection becomes node classification, and GNNExplainer shows which neighbors drove each decision.

For code, we predict which of two correct solutions to the same problem is faster, so machine and input effects cancel and only code structure remains. We built a dataset of 4,313,322 correct C++ solutions to 1,278 Codeforces problems, and a tree-based LSTM reads each solution's abstract syntax tree; we later learned structure-aware embeddings from these trees for performance prediction.

When data is scarce, PerfGen synthesizes tabular performance samples and scores them with Dissimilarity, a metric we designed to track downstream model accuracy. To give LLM-based generators the context that abbreviated column names lack, we tested expert-guided, LLM-guided, and Novel-Mapping prompts.
impact:
Across ten HPC datasets from three supercomputing facilities, and with up to 25% of values randomly missing, PinG embeddings cut MSE by up to 61.67% on HPC data and 78.56% on ML data over a DNN baseline. On Chimbuko traces from the Grid lattice-QCD code, GraphSAGE classified anomalies with 95% accuracy against 80% for XGBoost, and across 5 HPC and 6 ML datasets graph-based anomaly classification beat gradient-based methods in 6 of 11 experiments.

The code models predicted whether a solution is faster or slower up to 84% of the time when trained on a single problem and 73% when trained on 100 problems, against 68.5% for the best graph convolutional network; the labeled corpus of 4.3 million solutions is released for the community.

Across three performance datasets and five ML datasets, Dissimilarity correlated with model accuracy better than SD quality, KL divergence, and TabSyndex. With enriched prompts, models trained on synthetic data reached the baseline's quality in under 25% of the baseline's training epochs, and on the Parkinson's diagnosis dataset they cut random-forest MSE by more than 80%.

problem: Before an application can be optimized or autotuned, someone has to find out how it interacts with the hardware: which caches, memory paths, and stalls drive its execution time. Hardware performance counters record these interactions, but a modern GPU exposes hundreds of them. Developers and autotuners also usually judge an optimization only by execution time, so they do not see whether it leaves the GPU's streaming multiprocessors (SMs) idle.
importance: Idle SMs are compute capacity that could be doing science, and systems keep adding more accelerators per node. An optimization that lowers execution time can still waste the device, and one that raises utilization can slow the application down, so both need to be measured together. Autotuners such as GPTune recommend parameter values without saying why they work. Users therefore cannot learn which bottleneck a setting removed or apply that lesson to the next code.
challenges: Collecting the data is itself hard: NVIDIA's CUPTI instruments every kernel in a CUDA module, so its overhead grows with the number of kernels, and not all events can be counted at once. No utility listed which events can be collected together for a given GPU and CUDA version, so users grouped counters by hand. Analysis is the second obstacle, because tools such as nvprof report raw, timestamped counts without saying which resource matters statistically for a target metric. PCA-style reduction mixes counters into new features, so its output no longer names a resource a developer can fix. Counter names also differ across tools and systems, which rules out a fixed mapping from counters to hardware resources.
approach:
We built LIBNVCD on top of CUPTI: it needs three function calls in the source, lets users pick which kernels to profile and how often, and finds on its own which events can be measured together.

To analyze the counts, we use DASHING, which groups counters by hardware resource (L1, L2, DRAM, system memory, stalls) and uses ensemble Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, a sparse-coding method, to score each resource by how well its counters predict a target metric. We designed a composite target that combines execution time and SM utilization, characterized six common optimizations of matrix multiplication on an NVIDIA V100 with it, and turned the resource-usage patterns into a table of optimization suggestions. We then used those suggestions to find and apply optimizations in the ECP proxy applications Pennant and MiniFE and the MixBench benchmark.

To reach autotuner users, we integrated DASHING into GPTune with a user-guided, substring-based mapping of counters to groups, so it accepts counters from any collection tool. We applied the same characterization to Gradient Descent, AdaGrad, and ADAM optimizers training three RNN architectures on AMD MI100 GPUs.

We also built a programmable framework that analyzes performance measurements and shows them in a web-based interactive dashboard for exploring large hierarchical data.
impact: LIBNVCD adds a mean overhead below 1% over raw CUPTI, sets up 500x faster and cleans up 13x faster than hand-written CUPTI code, and is publicly released; compressing its counters into fewer features improved regression-based runtime prediction by up to 13%. On Pennant's Main3 kernel, optimizations chosen from the resource analysis improved execution time by up to 29.6% (27.4% on average) and SM utilization by up to 5.4%, and on the Leblancx input they lowered power draw by 12.2% on average. In GPTune, the analysis of 410 Hypre runs on 32 Cori Haswell nodes showed that two of the three grid-size parameters (nx, nz) track runtime while ny does not. On MI100 GPUs, it identified non-uniform memory access as the most frequent issue across the RNN optimizers. The dashboard helped us identify and fix problematic resource-usage behavior in three Exascale Computing Project applications.

problem: We define performance reproducibility as minimal run-to-run variation in execution time when the same application runs with the same configuration on the same system. On shared HPC systems this variation comes from network contention, power caps, task placement, and interference from other jobs, and in task-based workflows also from the scheduler changing task order from run to run. The users and administrators who choose these settings do not know which of them matters most, or which data they would need to explain a slow run afterwards.
importance: Variation makes 'fastest configuration' a moving target. A setting that gives the lowest average time can also give the widest spread, so users cannot plan allocations or compare results. The configuration space is also large: five user- and system-level knobs on one cluster already give 540 combinations to test. Workflows that combine simulation, analytics, and machine learning on DOE leadership systems add more layers where variation can enter, and the data needed to trace it is rarely kept in a findable, reusable form.
challenges: Earlier studies looked at one source of variation at a time, such as power or network traffic, and found influential parameters by sweeping the whole space, while feature-selection methods like recursive feature elimination need prior knowledge of the data model. For workflows, the tools that record performance data (Darshan for I/O, Chimbuko for trace anomalies, RADICAL-Cybertools for task execution) were not designed to work together: their data formats and meanings do not match, and naive conversion between them adds large overhead. Metadata and provenance are usually added after the run, piece by piece, so the information that would explain a divergent run is often missing. At the GPU level, a single trace can reach hundreds of gigabytes per run, and existing analysis tools read it sequentially into one node's memory.
approach:
To measure what causes variation, we collected a dataset on a 324-node production cluster at LLNL that varies node count, cores per node, network bandwidth level, power cap, and rank placement for five benchmarks while an interfering job runs. We defined a desirability score that rewards both low average time and low variation, and an influence score based on graph signal analysis, which does not depend on a specific model, that ranks which parameters make execution time predictable.

To keep the data needed to explain variation, we designed a pipeline in the DOE RECUP project that carries performance metadata from collection through curation, streaming, indexing, and analysis by combining RADICAL-Cybertools, Darshan, Chimbuko, Mochi, and DataStates, and stores it as RO-Crate so it meets FAIR principles. For Dask workflows, we extended Dask.distributed to stream task provenance through Mochi's Mofka service and adapted Darshan to record thread-level I/O, both into one table with shared identifiers.

To find causes inside GPU traces, we split Nsight traces into time shards that MPI ranks analyze in parallel, flag high-variability intervals with the inter-quartile range, and fit causal graphs that link kernel launch and memory features to run-to-run variation. To remove I/O cost from workflow stages we cannot modify, FILCIO intercepts C stdio calls and gathers small writes in memory before they reach disk.
impact: On the 324-node cluster, the influence analysis showed that network bandwidth level most affects repeatability and cut the configurations a user must evaluate for a new strong-scaling application by up to 97%; the finding held two years later for CG and miniAMR, after system and software upgrades. In a Dask XGBoost workflow on Polaris, the combined provenance and I/O data linked long-running I/O-fused tasks, larger than Dask's recommended 128 MB, to 297 unresponsive-event-loop warnings in the first 500 seconds. The distributed GPU-trace analysis ran 67% faster at 1,024 MPI ranks than at 128 (80 s versus 240 s) on four concurrent traces of about 93 million samples each, and showed that larger grid dimensions and device-to-device copies go with more kernel variability. FILCIO gave a 1.75x speedup on a program that spends nearly all of its runtime writing to disk.

problem: Edge nodes now combine CPUs with integrated GPUs and other accelerators, and streaming deep learning inference must run on them within deadlines. Using one device at a time, or splitting jobs evenly across devices, leaves capacity unused because each device performs differently on the same model. We ask how to assign inference jobs across the devices of one node so that the node meets its deadlines with the least time spent.
importance: Most research scales inference across distributed edge clouds and leaves the heterogeneous resources inside each node underutilized. Using those resources well gives more inference throughput from hardware that is already deployed. Device speed on an edge node also changes over time with thermal and power-management effects, so a schedule that meets deadlines at one moment can miss them later.
challenges: On-node scheduling had received less attention than cross-node scaling, so no scheduler divided a streaming inference workload across a node's CPU and integrated GPU under deadlines. Assigning jobs to devices with different speeds is a combinatorial problem, and heuristics such as genetic algorithms or task partitioning do not guarantee the best assignment. Because device speed drifts with temperature and power state, schedules must adapt, but existing adaptive schedulers recompute mappings online with heuristic search or learning, and that overhead grows with workload size.
approach: We first introduced a heterogeneous hyperperiod, based on the cyclic executive used in real-time systems: each device gets the same time in every window, and jobs are scheduled inside those windows. We then formulated rate monotonic scheduling across heterogeneous devices as an integer linear program, which finds optimal task assignments for streaming applications with deadlines. Most recently, we separated optimization from operation: we discretize each device's health using normalized frequency, power, and utilization, build a table of schedulable job assignments offline for every health combination, and at runtime adapt by switching tables in constant time.
impact: The heterogeneous-hyperperiod scheduler improved AlexNet and GoogLeNet-v1 image-classification performance by 1.5% to 48.1% compared with running on each device alone or splitting jobs evenly. The ILP-based rate monotonic scheduler improved inference efficiency by up to 5.26% over genetic-algorithm and task-partition scheduling, and it received the Best Paper Award at IEEE Cloud Summit 2025. The offline, health-indexed scheduler reduced runtime scheduling overhead by about 28x compared with heuristic-search and learning-based adaptive schedulers on multi-stream workloads (IEEE Cloud Summit 2026, 34.4% acceptance rate).

problem: The methods we build for performance data, such as learning from few labeled samples and reconstructing a large space from a small sample, also answer questions outside HPC. A counselor wants to know when a student's stress is about to rise, a fall-detection model must work for each person who wears it, and a biochemist needs to know which pairs of amino-acid mutations change a protein's structure. In each case, labeled data is scarce and the space of possibilities is too large to measure exhaustively.
importance: Autistic college students have a higher dropout rate than neurotypical students, and high physiological distress, depression, and anxiety are among the main causes. A model that predicts the onset of stress from wearable signals could support real-time intervention. A fall-detection model that works on average can still miss how one person moves, and collecting many labeled falls from each person is not practical. In structural biology, wet-lab mutation experiments can take months for even a small set of mutants, and the effect of two mutations cannot be predicted by adding the effects of each one alone.
challenges: Physiological data from wearables comes with few reliable stress labels, and autistic and neurotypical students may respond differently. Personalization runs into the problem our transfer-learning work addresses in HPC: the target has too few samples to train a model from scratch. For protein mutations, the number of mutants grows combinatorially: a 99-residue protein has 1,751,211 unique mutants with two substitutions. Even fast computational screening becomes intractable, and most existing methods only reason about single mutations.
approach:
For stress, we ran a mixed-method study that collected physiological and contextual data from mobile and wearable devices worn by 20 college students (10 autistic, 10 neurotypical), and combined unsupervised representation learning with semi-supervised label approximation to predict the onset of stress. For falls, ModelXc extends ModelX, our transfer-learning method for datasets whose features do not match, from regression to classification, and uses it to personalize fall-detection models from few samples per person.

For protein mutations, we generated every mutant with two amino-acid substitutions for 8 proteins and scored each with rigidity analysis to form a ground truth, then sampled a fraction of the mutants and rebuilt the full impact map under a low-rank constraint that smooths sampling noise. A later book chapter extended these low-rank approximation methods.

ACAC applies our systems methods to scientific simulation: it generates parallel MPI+OpenMP, MPI+CUDA, and MPI+HIP code for cellular-automata simulations, which model material diffusion and the spread of fire or disease, with no programming effort from users. Eunomia avoids interference among wireless medical devices by switching channels proactively and letting low-priority devices defer to safety-critical ones.
impact: The stress models predicted stress onset with 69% accuracy for autistic students, 72% for neurotypical students, and 70% for both groups together. The mutation study showed that the effect of two substitutions can be approximately predicted from as few as 25% of all mutations, and the low-rank constraint reduced the reconstruction error by up to 34% for one protein (1pga). For a cellular automaton with 2.36M cells, ACAC's generated code ran up to 544.2x faster than a sequential baseline on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and up to 16.8x faster than a specialized FPGA implementation, and it scales cellular-automata simulations up to 10 billion cells.

problem: Large systems are only as usable as the software that connects scientists to them. Storage must keep up as node counts grow, researchers need one path to many computing resources, monitoring pipelines need analysis that runs as fast as the data arrives, and hardware designers need to evaluate chips that do not exist yet. We build that software.
importance: Distributed burst buffers give aggregate storage bandwidth that grows linearly with node count, but only if metadata keeps pace. The Network for Earthquake Engineering Simulation (NEES) spans 14 labs across the USA whose researchers need XSEDE, the Open Science Grid, and Purdue supercomputers. In-situ monitoring such as Chimbuko records provenance databases with up to more than 16M anomaly entries, which no one can read by hand.
challenges: Metadata for files shared across many processes must be tracked in a global index that thousands of processes access at once, so metadata management becomes the performance limit. Chimbuko's HBOS detector keeps histograms per function, and extending it to hundreds of counters would create hundreds of bins per counter that must be synchronized over the network. Each computing venue has its own submission interface, so researchers would otherwise have to learn every one.
approach: MetaKV adds metadata services to an existing key-value store for the bursty, concurrent metadata workloads of distributed burst buffers: compressed storage management, supervised block clustering, and log-ring based collective message reduction. BatchSubmit lets NEES researchers run on XSEDE, the Open Science Grid, Purdue supercomputers, and NEEShub servers through the NEEShub science gateway. For Chimbuko, we treat anomalies as noise in a signal and detect them with FFT, which keeps memory and network traffic low, and we built a visual tool in the DASHING framework for exploring anomaly provenance databases. We also built a tool that automatically generates mixed-precision programs, and GpNoCSim, a general-purpose simulator for networks-on-chip that we later extended.
impact: MetaKV sped up metadata put and get operations by up to 2.66x and 6.29x over state-of-the-art key-value stores, and its benefit grows with metadata load. The FFT detector improved accuracy x F1 per unit overhead by up to 99% on benchmark datasets and up to 93% on Chimbuko traces. The visual tool lets users explore provenance databases with 200K to more than 16M anomaly entries in a few seconds.

problem: Recent workforce efforts prepare students to write programs for heterogeneous HPC platforms, but computation is only one of the three tasks an HPC application performs; the other two are communication and I/O. More broadly, AI is changing how scientific software is built and who builds it, and the institutions and training pipelines behind scientific computing have to change with it.
importance: Network bandwidth is not scaling with compute, so moving the data these applications generate slows scientific progress. The problem of scaling data-intensive applications is common to high-performance, high-throughput, and cloud computing, so training in it has broad reach. Community-level plans matter because no single lab or university can set training and collaboration practices for the whole scientific computing ecosystem.
challenges: A data-driven analysis of existing curricula shows that most do not prepare students to consider the design choices that scale parallel I/O, a crucial part of an end-to-end system. Teaching it requires hands-on access to systems where I/O actually becomes the bottleneck, not only programming exercises.
approach: We designed HPC@SCALE, a hands-on course at Texas State University that trains students to build scalable end-to-end system software with a focus on minimizing parallel I/O. We also take part in the Next-Generation Ecosystems for Scientific Computing (NGE) workshop series, a three-year series on building scientific computing ecosystems through socio-technical co-design: the intentional integration of social and technical components as parts of one strategy.
impact: HPC@SCALE was presented as an invited paper at the EduHiPC workshop at HiPC 2021. The 2025 NGE workshop convened more than 40 experts from national laboratories, academia, industry, and community organizations, and its report recommends modular, trustworthy AI-enabled scientific software and training pipelines that keep pace with technological change. The 2026 report turns four strategic themes, including workforce, pedagogy, and governance, into eight priorities for community action.

problem: Production science codes are often too large, too complex to set up, or too restricted to distribute for early hardware design studies, so co-design teams use proxy applications that extract one performance-critical kernel. XSBench, for example, extracts the macroscopic cross-section lookup that accounts for about 85% of OpenMC's runtime. A proxy is only useful if it stresses the hardware the way its parent does, and there was no quantitative way to check that.
importance: Architects and procurement teams make decisions from proxy measurements. If a proxy misses a resource bottleneck that limits its parent, those decisions rest on the wrong behavior. A coverage measure tells developers whether the existing proxies are enough or whether a new proxy is needed to cover a missing resource.
challenges: Earlier validation, including our own XSBench study, correlated each hardware counter with efficiency loss one counter at a time. Correlation does not imply causation, and a one-at-a-time analysis cannot find a group of counters that together explain performance. PCA and CCA handle groups, but they build new features by mixing counters, so the result no longer names a resource a developer can act on. The counters also differ by architecture, so a per-counter comparison on Intel Xeon does not carry over to IBM Blue Gene/Q.
approach:
We first built XSBench with Argonne's CESAR team and verified it against OpenMC using 47 hardware counters on Intel Xeon.

We then built VERITAS, which asks two questions for each hardware resource: how much does this resource predict the parent's loss of parallel efficiency, and how well does the proxy reproduce the parent's use of it. For the first question, we fit a sparse model of efficiency loss over all counters and add up the belief of every counter in a resource group into one Resource Significance Measure (RSM). For the second, we build a low-dimensional subspace from each application's counters for that resource and measure how close the two subspaces are, which gives a Coverage score between 0 and 1. Because both scores are per resource group rather than per counter, they compare the same resources across architectures and still report the individual counters behind each score. PADDLE, a general ML framework for HPC performance data, later automated the same coverage workflow with learned features.
impact: XSBench's multi-core scaling efficiency and floating-point rate fall within 5% of OpenMC's; at 16 threads, efficiency drops to 66% in OpenMC and 69% in XSBench. VERITAS showed that XSBench covers 80% of OpenMC's memory behavior on Xeon and 90% of its L2 behavior on Blue Gene/Q. It also showed that RSBench, which cuts memory use from 5.6 GB to 41 MB by recomputing data, covers only about 75% of OpenMC's memory behavior on Xeon, and that CMT-Bone's point-compute kernel covers all but one of CMT-nek's resource behaviors. PADDLE reproduced the published XSBench coverage result through its automated pipeline. The DOE Exascale Computing Project adopted XSBench as the standard proxy for OpenMC. Applying the same methodology, we found that the CMT-Bone proxy developed by the NNSA PSAAP II center for NEK5000 did not match its parent's behavior and guided its remediation, so the team did not optimize a proxy that misrepresented the target workload.

problem: MPI tools have long used the PMPI profiling interface, which only sees calls between the application and the MPI library, not what happens inside the library. MPI 3.0 added MPI_T to expose internal performance variables, such as unexpected message queue lengths, and control variables, such as eager limits, but users had no tools to read them. Separately, the MPI standard leaves MPI's state undefined after a process failure, so most applications can do little more than abort.
importance: Internal library behavior, such as which receive queue matches a message or how a protocol is configured, decides communication performance, yet it was invisible to users without implementation-specific hacks. A job script that records the library's configuration also lets users explain a performance change between runs. On the resilience side, process failures usually terminate the whole application, so a practical recovery model is required for MPI codes to keep running on large systems.
challenges: MPI_T was designed after PERUSE failed standardization because PERUSE defined internal events that did not match every implementation. MPI_T therefore defines no variables at all: each library decides what to expose, so a tool cannot know in advance which variables exist and must discover them at run time. For fault tolerance, the ULFM proposal supplies failure detection and communicator repair, but using it needs large code changes, because most applications create communicators in many places. Error codes and error handlers also do not tell the programmer where in the code a failure happened, and the transactional FA-MPI works only for non-blocking operations.
approach:
We wrote a user's introduction to MPI_T and built two tools on it. Varlist queries and lists every control and performance variable a library exposes, so a job script can record the exact MPI configuration of a run. Gyan is a lightweight profiler that attaches to all performance variables, or a user-chosen subset, reads them at start and end, and reports the sum, minimum, and maximum across ranks. We applied both tools to the NAS BT benchmark and to NEK5000 on Open MPI and MVAPICH2.

In FTA, programmers wrap MPI calls for a set of ranks in a TRY block; at the end of the block all ranks agree on whether a failure occurred, so the failure is localized to that block. FTA tracks every communicator created through PMPI wrappers and repairs all of them automatically in either shrinking mode or non-shrinking mode with spare processes, and a RETRY statement restarts the block.
impact: Monitoring all MPI_T performance variables with Gyan changed average run time by less than 0.5%, below the noise threshold, and Varlist lists every variable of MVAPICH2-2.0a in 1 second. On BT, Gyan showed that larger problem sizes push more messages through the unexpected receive queue, which points to specific receives to reschedule. On NEK5000, Gyan showed that MVAPICH2's blocking mode, which saves polling cycles, raises run time by 28% at 64 processes. We demonstrated FTA's shrinking and non-shrinking recovery on a synthetic code and on the CoMD molecular dynamics proxy application.

problem: Long-running simulations stay productive only if a failure costs little work and a power limit costs little speed. Checkpoint/restart handles failures by saving state periodically, but saving state is expensive: on shared Condor grids checkpoints travel long distances to a few dedicated servers, and on supercomputers thousands of processes write to one parallel file system at once. Power limits add a second cost, because a job held to a fixed per-node bound slows down during computation even though it leaves power unused while it writes checkpoints or other I/O.
importance: When checkpoints are expensive, applications checkpoint less often, and each failure then throws away more computation. Checkpointing already causes 75-80% of the I/O traffic on HPC systems, and compute capability is growing faster than I/O bandwidth. On a power-limited system, power left idle during one job's I/O phase is performance that another job could have used.
challenges: On grids, using the spare disks of volunteer machines removes the central server, but those hosts leave, get loaded by their owners, or fail, and earlier failure models covered only compute hosts, not storage hosts. On supercomputers, general-purpose compressors gain little on scientific data, and merging checkpoints from many processes in rank order does not place similar data together. Lossy compression shrinks checkpoints 3 to 5 times, but no one knew whether a simulation restarted from an inexact state still gives a correct answer. For power, earlier work shifted power only among the nodes of a single job, and shifting across jobs needs to know when each job's I/O phases start, how long they last, and which job can take the power.
approach:
For grids, we built FALCON, which stores checkpoints on the disks of the grid's own machines. FALCON models each storage host with multiple failure states, predicts which hosts will stay available and lightly loaded, and splits each checkpoint into erasure-coded fragments so it can be rebuilt from a subset of hosts.

For supercomputers, we built McrEngine, which reads the metadata in HDF5 and netCDF checkpoints, groups variables with the same name and type across processes, and compresses each group with the algorithm that works best for that group. Aggregating on a few nodes also cuts the number of concurrent writers to the parallel file system. We then tested lossy checkpoint compression on the ChaNGa cosmology code by injecting failures and checking the physical output.

For power, we designed algorithms that move power from a job in an I/O phase to jobs in computation phases, including a scheduler that staggers jobs so fewer do I/O at the same time. We evaluated them in PowerShifter, a simulator validated against a real-cluster prototype running Cactus, ParaDiS, and LAMMPS.
impact: On Purdue's production Condor pool of 20,000 processors, FALCON improved application performance by 11% to 44% over Condor's checkpointing with local and remote storage servers; the SC09 paper was a Best Student Paper Finalist. McrEngine improved compression by up to 115% over concatenate-and-compress, cut checkpoint overhead by up to 87% and restart overhead by up to 62%, and was an SC12 Best Student Paper Finalist. Mixing 16- and 32-bit lossy compression with gzip shrank ChaNGa checkpoints to 15% of their original size, while 32-bit lossy checkpoints gave correct results for 3 to 70 injected failures. I/O-aware power shifting improved average performance by up to 8% and a single high-priority job by up to 32%, and PowerShifter predicted run times within 2% of real runs. McrEngine's aggregation and compression methods are now integrated into the Scalable Checkpoint/Restart (SCR) library, which won an R&D 100 award in 2019 and supports LLNL's El Capitan exascale system, and FALCON was deployed on Purdue's campus grid.
